Heatwave Drought

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As heat waves hit Gauteng, the water levels of the Vaal dam continue to drop... Will Gauteng have to face DAY ZERO in the near future?

Unique Selling Point:
The Katse Dam is standing at 13% and the Vaal dam is at about 50% and yet The Department of Water and Sanitation says there is no need to panic. And levels of the Vaal are said to drop further in light of the current heatwave across most of the country. Climate Experts are saying that we should expect below normal rainfall and higher than normal temperatures, which means that our dams will be losing more water, quicker. Yet there seems to be no sense of urgency amongst Government and municipalities. People are watering gardens and washing cars as if there is absolutely nothing to worry about. Spokesperson for the DWS, Sputnik Ratau said the Vaal Dam forms part of an integrated river system, which supplies water to the majority of residents in Gauteng as well as Eskom power stations, and taking all the dams in the system into account.

Summary:
It's October. It's hot and dusty in Gauteng. "When will the rains come?" is a question Gautengers impatiently ask around this time of year. Traditionally Farmers used President Paul Kruger's birthday (10 October) as the start of the rainy season, but with Climate Change the seasons are shifting and Gauteng's rain comes later and later. Add to that the incredible heatwaves and you would understand that some people are panicking about Gauteng's water supply. The Vaal dam has a very large surface area and water is rapidly evaporating. The levels are currently just above 50% compared to 81% during the same period last year. On top of that the Katse Dam, which feeds water to the Vaal System is alarmingly low - at 13%. And they are doing maintenance on the Lesotho Highlands Pipe networks, which means that additional water can only be pumped to SA from the end of November. In the meantime the weather forecast predicts less than average rainfall for the next few months and hotter temperatures than the average. All this is spelling doom for Gauteng's water supply.

The Department of Water and Sanitation states that there is no reason to panic: “When we look at the Integrated Vaal River System, we see a combination of about 14 dams that primarily serve Gauteng and standing at about 73.7%. This is a decline, which is quite huge because about a week ago, we were standing at about 76%.”

Further information:
For the 2017/18 financial year the Auditor General found that every province in the country lost money through failing water infrastructure...
The Eastern Cape – R591 million;
Free State – R260 million;
Northern Cape – R112 million;
North West – R124 million;
KwaZulu-Natal – just over R1 million;
Western Cape – R10 million;
Limpopo – R154 million
Gauteng – just under R3 million; and
Mpumalanga – R407 million

It’s almost been 11 months since the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) was deployed to the Vaal region help rehabilitate the river. Various state bodies and government leaders have made commitments (both monetary and non-monetary) to rebuild the system, money has been channelled to “operation Vaal River”, yet non-profit organisation Save the Vaal Environment (SAVE) has raised concerns over the project and whether it is receiving enough financial support.

Car rental to drive to Lesothoo and the Freestate

Heatwave Drought Script




Claire LINK
It’s the end of October and in the Summer rainfall regions of South Africa we’re all looking to the skies to see when the first significant rains will come, but for most parts of the country it’s just hot and dry.
v/o
While the welcoming sounds of thunderstorms stay away, our water reservoirs are feeling the pressure and many of our smaller dams have dried up. Even the Vaal dam, which services Gauteng, parts of the Free State, Mpumalanga and Northwest is a cause for concern. Persistent heatwaves and dry winds, coupled with increased demand and the lack of rain has led to a significant drop in water levels.
Kathy Manten
We have dropped in excess of 3% within 5 days….
V/O
Kathy Manten owns and runs a local marina on the Vaal dam, and says the situation is worrisome.
Kathy Manten
With the Vaal river system at 50% and no guarantee of when we’re going to get water, Joburg is in a real crisis.
V/O
Manten Marina is already pulling some of the bigger boats out of the water, as this will be impossible once the water levels have dropped further.
Kathy Manten
But while those boats are out of the water they’re not being used, the owners are not coming down to their boats. They’re not breaking their boats, which means the industries that fix, repair, renovate, make boats pretty, are not getting any work and the staff of those companies in turn are going to be hurting because you can’t just keep on going with your doors open and no money coming in.
V/o
And it’s not just the boating industry that is suffering. Towns all along the dam are seeing a drop in tourism which affects the entire community.
LINK
The Vaal dam was constructed in 1938 and is about 47 metres deep. It holds 995 million cubic metres of water but right now it’s less than half full. Is that enough water for Gauteng for the foreseeable future?
V/O
Spokesperson for the Department of Water and Sanitation, Sputnik Ratau says the situation is serious compared to last year when the dam was about 92% full. During October 2016 the Vaal dam dropped to about 27% but at the current levels, Ratau says, there is no reason to panic.
Sputnik Ratau
We’re also coming out of the winter and winter is not a rainy season for the inland provinces.
V/O
But climatologists paint a dire picture of the country- and region’s rainfall for the short, and long term future...
Francois Engelbrecht
As we are nearing the end of October 2019 South Africa is gripped in a state of drought. We are looking at conditions of at least mild drought almost across the entire South Africa because over the last 3 years rainfall was below normal across most of the country.
V/O
Professor Francois Engelbrecht from the Global Change Institute at WITS is an expert in the field of Climate Modelling and spoke to us via skype from Melbourne, Australia. He explains that when the high pressure systems across the interior of the country are very strong and they persist well into spring then we usually see this late onset of summer rainfall.


Francois Engelbrecht
And when a high-pressure system becomes exceptionally strong it causes a lot of sinking air over the country and that means that cloud formation is almost completely suppressed and that is the type of weather pattern that brings heat waves to the Southern African region.
v/o
And the really alarming fact is that climate models predict that our region will just get drier and hotter as climate change continues to accelerate… And Southern Africa is warming at double the global average . This year, the month of September was declared the hottest on record. Temperatures are equal only to September 2016, which was an El Nino year.
Jennifer Fitchett
We’re talking about the whole world being warmer, so the countries where September is toward the end of their Winter and moving into their Spring, we’d expect it to start warming up, but that’s warmer than our Spring.
V/O
Senior Lecturer at Wits, Dr Jennifer Fitchett specialises in the impacts of climate change on both the natural environment and human populations.
Jennifer Fitchett
What we're looking at is a global scale increase in heat. We're not looking at a redistribution of the heat budget where some place is now a degree colder everywhere is warmer than it has been on record.
V/o
So what does a hotter and drier future mean for South Africa? And specifically for Gauteng, the industrial hub of SA, which gets its water from the rapidly shrinking Vaal dam?
Sputnik Ratau
The fact that the Vaal dam is at just below 50 doesn’t necessarily mean that Gauteng is running out of water.

Okay

The thing is that the vaal dam is one dam of but 14 dams that comprise what we call the Integrated Vaal River System.
V/O
The Integrated Vaal River System gets 73% of its water from catchments in Mpumalanga, North West, Free State and the Northern Cape. The other other 27% comes from the Katse dam via the Lesotho Highland Water Project…

Currently the entire system is just below 60% full.
Sputnik Ratau
Claire: Are you saying that people shouldn’t be worried yet?

People must always be worried about water availability in South Africa because we are in a region that is arid.
V/O
Adding to the concern over Gauteng’s water, is the fact that the Katse dam is only about 13% full.
LINK
Last year the water levels at the Katse dam reached this mark here that is easily visible. On Monday we took a trip to Lesotho to see where the water level was and this is what we found.
V/O
The dam levels are exceptionally low. The Malibamatso river is providing little relief for the people and streams coming down from the peaks are barely trickling...
Sputnik Ratau
You must remember Lesotho has also been experiencing the same drought. So Katse dam would be low because the water levels in Lesotho are low anyway.
V/O
On the 1st of October the water from Katse was shut down for 2 months for scheduled maintenance, and as a result very little water is coming into the Vaal dam.
Kathy Manten
Our inflow at the dam has gone down from about 18 cubic metres a second to approximately 0.5 cubic metres a second.
V/O
According to Ratau the shutdown was planned for well in advance.
Sputnik Ratau
They had made provision for the amount of water that would have flowed through in the 2 months of the shutdown to be in the system, in the Integrated Vaal System before the shutdown happened on the 1st of October.
LINK
Downstream from the Vaal dam the effects of the drought are not quite as evident on the Vaal river, the water levels remain fairly constant because of the water released from the dam.
V?O
The sluice gates remain open, releasing water for downstream users of the river… but the residents along the banks of the Vaal have a whole different set of problems which are exacerbated by the drought and heat...
Kas Lubbe
Claire: I don’t think we’ve ever smelt something this bad. But you seem okay. Is this the normal small?

Claire, Welcome to the Vaal, in the first place.
V/O
The ongoing sewage and wastewater crisis in the Vaal has left people like Kas Lubbe desperate for relief. Despite the SANDF being deployed a year ago to help solve the crisis at Emfuleni Municipality, the situation seems to be deteriorating.
Kas Lubbe
Claire: I just want to know then, has the drought made it worse?

Yes. Definitely. Normally rain help us that some of this stuff gets washed away.

Claire: I actually can’t stand here any longer. Can we leave?


Kathy Manten
Just to cap it all the DWS is letting out tonnes of water every couple of weeks to flush the pollution out of the rivers. 40 cubic metres per second to flow down out of the Vaal dam, 40 cubic meters per second of good water to flush the poo out the river.
Sputnik Ratau
It is not correct to say we are flushing the river with potable water. There is no water that is in a dam that is already potable. So the water that flows out of the Vaal dam still remains in the system. So that is not water that is lost. It is water that remains in the system until it goes into the treatment works then it becomes potable.
V/O
According to predictions our significant Summer rainfall will only come in December, and no-one can say for sure whether we’ll have a normal or below average rainy season, but everyone is in agreement that the time has come for us to change the way in which we use water.
Jennifer Fitchett
Claire: Should we be worried about the fact that the Vaal dam is just below 50 percent full.
So there are mixed messages on this and I know that there have been messages from government that we shouldn't worry just yet. My feeling is it's better to be cautious. I think that at the point where the Vaal dam is at 50 percent we should be really trying to limit our water consumption as much as possible.
Francois Engelbrecht
That means that the responsible thing for South Africans to do right now -- for the water managers, for our farmers, but also for the general public is to plan for another season that may well be dry, and for us as ordinary members of the public it means we need to contribute our fair share in saving as much water as we can.




PROMO 1 11”
Persistent heatwaves, hot dry winds and a lack of significant downpour in our Summer rainfall regions… what does all this mean for the economic and industrial hub of South Africa?




PROMO 2 11”
South Africa is currently gripped in a drought and experts say the Summer rains are still a while away. At just below 50%, how long can the Vaal system sustain Gauteng and the neighbouring regions?




PROMO 3 11”
A series of extreme heatwaves and persistent drought throughout the Summer rainfall area of South Africa… How is Climate Change affecting Gauteng’s water supply? Are we heading for disaster?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Katse Dam is standing at 13% and the Vaal dam is at about 50% and yet The Department of Water and Sanitation says there is no need to panic. And levels of the Vaal are said to drop further in light of the current heatwave across most of the country. Climate Experts are saying that we should expect below normal rainfall and higher than normal temperatures, which means that our dams will be losing more water, quicker. Yet there seems to be no sense of urgency amongst Government and municipalities. People are watering gardens and washing cars as if there is absolutely nothing to worry about. Spokesperson for the DWS, Sputnik Ratau said the Vaal Dam forms part of an integrated river system, which supplies water to the majority of residents in Gauteng as well as Eskom power stations, and taking all the dams in the system into account.
metadata.Summary: It's October. It's hot and dusty in Gauteng. "When will the rains come?" is a question Gautengers impatiently ask around this time of year. Traditionally Farmers used President Paul Kruger's birthday (10 October) as the start of the rainy season, but with Climate Change the seasons are shifting and Gauteng's rain comes later and later. Add to that the incredible heatwaves and you would understand that some people are panicking about Gauteng's water supply. The Vaal dam has a very large surface area and water is rapidly evaporating. The levels are currently just above 50% compared to 81% during the same period last year. On top of that the Katse Dam, which feeds water to the Vaal System is alarmingly low - at 13%. And they are doing maintenance on the Lesotho Highlands Pipe networks, which means that additional water can only be pumped to SA from the end of November. In the meantime the weather forecast predicts less than average rainfall for the next few months and hotter temperatures than the average. All this is spelling doom for Gauteng's water supply. The Department of Water and Sanitation states that there is no reason to panic: “When we look at the Integrated Vaal River System, we see a combination of about 14 dams that primarily serve Gauteng and standing at about 73.7%. This is a decline, which is quite huge because about a week ago, we were standing at about 76%.”
metadata.Further information: For the 2017/18 financial year the Auditor General found that every province in the country lost money through failing water infrastructure... The Eastern Cape – R591 million; Free State – R260 million; Northern Cape – R112 million; North West – R124 million; KwaZulu-Natal – just over R1 million; Western Cape – R10 million; Limpopo – R154 million Gauteng – just under R3 million; and Mpumalanga – R407 million It’s almost been 11 months since the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) was deployed to the Vaal region help rehabilitate the river. Various state bodies and government leaders have made commitments (both monetary and non-monetary) to rebuild the system, money has been channelled to “operation Vaal River”, yet non-profit organisation Save the Vaal Environment (SAVE) has raised concerns over the project and whether it is receiving enough financial support.
